explanations.explanation: The sand of the sea, friend. Go ahead and try counting that at the beach. You'll quit around grain number forty and just enjoy the view. The verse says it cannot be measured or counted (Hosea 1:10), and it comes right after all those hard words about "…not My people…"

I see why that one tempts you, but the verse never says tribes. It says the number will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. A tribe count is something you could write on a card. This promise is about a number nobody can write down.

Gates are the kind of thing you could count with a clipboard and a pencil. The verse never mentions them, though. It says the Israelites' number will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. Good luck with that clipboard.
Sons of the living God. Read that slowly, baker. In the very place where it was said, "You are not My people…" that's the new name they'll be called. Same spot, brand new label.

That one sounds like a rough turn, but it's not in the verse. The text says that in the very place where they were told they were not His people, they will be called "sons of the living God." The promise points up, not down. I think that's the whole surprise of the verse.

Not quite, friend. The verse never calls them strangers. It says that where they were told "You are not My people…" they will be called "sons of the living God." That's a name that brings them close, not one that keeps them outside.

Judah it is. The verse says the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together (Hosea 1:11). Two groups who were apart end up in one place. I think that's good news for anybody who's ever had a group chat go quiet.
Egypt isn't named in this verse, friend. Hosea 1:11 says the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together. So the blank is Judah. Egypt doesn't get a mention here.
Assyria isn't in this verse, friend. The promise says the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together (Hosea 1:11). Judah is the word that fits the blank. Assyria can sit this one out.

Close, but the verse says the opposite. Judah and Israel will appoint for themselves one leader, not many (Hosea 1:11). One leader. Anybody who's sat through a meeting with ten people steering the same car knows why that sounds like a gift.
False, and you caught it. The text says they will appoint for themselves one leader (Hosea 1:11). Not a committee, not a panel, just one. Picture a kitchen with one head baker. Things go smoother.
My people. That's what the LORD says to call the brothers (Hosea 2:1). Back in Hosea 1:10 the words were "…not My people…" Now the words are flipped around.
It's a fair guess, but servants isn't the word. The LORD says to say of your brothers, "My people." That's what Hosea 2:1 gives. It's a name that says they belong to Him.
Neighbors is friendly, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says to say of your brothers, "My people." That's the exact phrase in Hosea 2:1. It's closer than neighbors, if you ask me.

True. The LORD says to say of your sisters, "My loved one." Brothers get "My people" and sisters get "My loved one." and both names come in the same verse (Hosea 2:1). I think that's a lot of warmth packed into one line.
It's actually true. The verse says, "Say of your brothers, ‘My people,’ and of your sisters, ‘My loved one.’" That's right there in Hosea 2:1. So the sisters do get that name, and it's a good one.
That's it. The LORD wants her to remove the adultery and the unfaithfulness. He's saying that she is not His wife and He is not her husband. It's a hard verse, but the way out is right there in it.
The verse doesn't mention a crown or robes. The LORD says she should remove the adultery and the unfaithfulness. This isn't about her wardrobe, friend. It's about how she's been living.

The verse does say she is not His wife and He is not her husband, but that's not what the LORD wants removed. He wants the adultery and the unfaithfulness gone. Notice it's about her actions, not a name or a title.

Thirst. The LORD says He'll make her like a desert and a parched land, and let her die of thirst. I think this is a heavy one, so let's just take it seriously. The picture is of a dry, empty place with nothing to drink.

Hunger sounds close, but the verse says thirst. The LORD says He will make her like a desert and a parched land, and let her die of thirst. A desert fits that word. This is a heavy verse, so it helps to read it carefully.

The verse isn't about cold. It says He'll make her like a desert and a parched land, and let her die of thirst. A desert is dry, and that's what the word thirst matches. This is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

The verse says the opposite. The LORD says, "I will have no compassion on her children, because they are the children of adultery." That's the text, and it gives the reason right in the verse. It's a hard line to sit with.

False, and that's what the text says. The LORD says, "I will have no compassion on her children, because they are the children of adultery." The reason is in the verse itself. I think it's one of the heavy lines of this chapter.

Food and clothes, yes. She thought, "I will go after my lovers, who give me bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink." Bread, water, oil and drink are the food side, and wool and linen are the clothes. Notice it's what she thought. The next verses talk about what the LORD says He gave her.

A crown and throne would be quite a gift, but that's not her list. She thought her lovers gave her "…bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink." That's everyday stuff, like food and clothing. Plain needs, not royal ones.
No horses or chariots here, friend. Her words were, "I will go after my lovers, who give me bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink." That's food and clothing. Everyday things, not war gear.

explanations.answer: So she can't find her way
explanations.explanation: Right. He says He'll hedge up her path with thorns and enclose her with a wall, "…so she cannot find her way." Hedged with thorns, enclosed with a wall. That's a lot standing in her way.

explanations.answer: So her lovers can find her
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. The thorns and the wall are there so she cannot find her way. The next verse says she'll pursue her lovers but not catch them. So the hedge keeps her from them.

explanations.answer: So she can build a home
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about building a home. The LORD says He'll hedge up her path with thorns and enclose her with a wall, so she cannot find her way. A wall in the path is a blocker, not a blueprint. I wouldn't hang a picture on it.

The text says she won't catch them. "She will pursue her lovers but not catch them; she will seek them but not find them." Think of running for a bus while the doors are closing and the driver is waving. All that effort and nothing to show for it.

False, and you read it right. She will pursue her lovers but not catch them, and she will seek them but not find them (Hosea 2:7). Two verbs of chasing and two of coming up empty. It's like sprinting for the elevator and watching the doors close.

Husband. The verse says she will say, "I will return to my first husband…" That's a turn in her thinking, once she can't catch her lovers. It's the first time in this part that she talks about returning instead of chasing.
The verse doesn't mention a father. She says, "I will return to my first husband…" The picture all through this chapter is a marriage. So husband is the word that fits the blank.

Home sounds natural, but that's not her word. She will say, "I will return to my first husband…" She's not naming a place. She's naming a person, and that fits the marriage picture of the whole passage.

The LORD. He says it was He who gave her grain, new wine and oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold (Hosea 2:8). She does not acknowledge it. Not acknowledging who baked the cookies is awkward at any table.

Baal is in this verse, but he's not the giver. The LORD says it was He who gave her grain, new wine, and oil. The silver and gold He lavished on her is what they crafted for Baal, a false god. So the blank is LORD.
No king in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "…it was I who gave her grain, new wine, and oil…" Nobody else gets the credit line here. He's the one who gave it, so the blank is LORD.
Take them back. The LORD says, "…I will take back My grain in its time and My new wine in its season…" Notice He calls them "My" grain and "My" new wine. The gifts were His to begin with.
The verse goes the other direction. The LORD says He will take back His grain in its time and His new wine in its season. He also says He'll take away His wool and linen. So less, not more.
Judah isn't part of this verse's plan. The LORD says, "…I will take back My grain in its time and My new wine in its season…" It's taken back, not sent somewhere else. Keep an eye on the verb.

True. The LORD says the wool and linen "…were given to cover her nakedness." They were gifts with a purpose, and He's the one who gave them. When He says He'll take them away, that's the weight of it.
It's actually true. The text says the wool and linen "…were given to cover her nakedness." That's the LORD's own description in Hosea 2:9. So they were meant to cover her.

The verse says the opposite. The LORD says, "…no one will deliver her out of My hands." He says it just after saying He'll expose her lewdness in the sight of her lovers. That's the text, plain and simple.

False, and that's right. The LORD says He will expose her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one will deliver her out of His hands. Her lovers can't rescue her. I think that's the hard truth under all these lines.

Feasts and Sabbaths, yes. The LORD says He will put an end to all her exultation: her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths, all her appointed feasts. That's the whole calendar of celebrations. The list in the verse is long, so it's good to catch the right part.

Armies and walls aren't in this verse. The LORD says He'll end her exultation, and then names her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths. This is about celebrations, not defense. The list is all about the calendar.

Markets and trade don't appear in this verse. What the LORD puts an end to is her exultation: her feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths, all her appointed feasts. It's about the celebrations. The word to look for is feasts.

A thicket. The LORD says He'll destroy her vines and fig trees and make them into a thicket, and the beasts of the field will devour them. Vines and fig trees turned into a thicket is a heavy picture. I think this is one of the hard lines in this chapter.

A threshing floor is a working place, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says He'll make her vines and fig trees into a thicket. Then the beasts of the field will devour them. The word you want is thicket.

A courtyard sounds tidy, and the verse is the opposite. The LORD says He will make her vines and fig trees into a thicket, and the beasts of the field will devour them. That's wild growth, not neat stonework. It's more brush than building.
Forgot. The LORD ends the list with, "But Me she forgot…" declares the LORD. After all the rings, jewelry and incense, that's the line that sums it up. It's the heart of the whole speech.
Cursed isn't the word here. The verse closes with, "But Me she forgot…" declares the LORD. It's quieter than cursing, and I think it stings more. Forgetting is what the text says.
The verse doesn't say she fought Him. It says, "But Me she forgot…" declares the LORD. She was busy with the Baals, and she forgot Him. The word that fits the blank is forgot.
